So, after the Apollo landings, after we "beat the Russians", Congressional support for the space program collapsed. There were other priorities. Lyndon B Johnson had been a terrible president in many ways, but particularly in terms of economics. Unions struck, businesses closed, jobs were lost. The seeds of this disaster had been sown much earlier, due to the decision to run high corporate taxes and practically non-existent import tariffs in the aftermath of WW2. We did this to rebuild the economies of our allies, but we did so at our peril and by the 70's high tech manufacturing in other countries was starting to undercut us. Nixon's easing of relations with China didn't help either, and soon the textiles industry was in decline as well.

So, by the mid 1970's fair to say Congress had a lot on its hands. The Apollo Applications Program (of which the Skylab and the Apollo-Soyuz mission were but a mere fraction of the possible mission) had a lot of proposals but didn't stand to create many jobs, so beyond a token effort to match the Russians with a space station of our own, the Nixon administration basically let space slide as an issue.

Now, NASA knew what it would take to get Congress to buy into a new project, and that was a new vehicle with big fat development contracts for a lot of businesses in a lot of states. Hence, the Space Shuttle. Which was sold on two lies, one that it would be reusable and two that it would be cheap. It was neither. It also wasn't particularly safe. But Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter bought into those two lies and so we got that white elephant.

The shuttle was designed for one primary purpose: to build a space station.

Reagan was willing to keep throwing money at development of space station freedom but he wasn't willing to pull the trigger on construction, it was just too expensive. So we flew the shuttle 87 times before ever using it for the purpose for which it was intended (to build a space station).

Mir was aging and while there was great interest in Russia in maintaining the space program, they were of limited means. During the Clinton administration, NASA was able to come to terms that Congress could support. We would build a space station, using hardware we'd already partially built, with the Russians providing the parts we hadn't built equivalents for. Finally the Shuttle was able to perform its original purpose, whereupon we (wisely) yanked it from service before even completing a replacement.
